meta.titre: Alkanes and alkenes: structure, substitution, addition and polymers

sections.contenu_markdown: At the SONARA refinery in Limbe, crude oil is heated and separated into petrol, kerosene, diesel and the gas that fills the cooking cylinders sold in every town. The same crude oil also supplies the starting material for the polythene bags and plastic buckets in the market. All these products are built from hydrocarbons, compounds of carbon and hydrogen only. Two families, the alkanes and the alkenes, are tested every year at the GCE O/L, either as naming and formulae questions or as reactions such as substitution and addition polymerisation.

items: Carbon forms four covalent bonds and hydrogen forms one.
A hydrocarbon contains only carbon and hydrogen atoms.
Crude oil is separated into fractions by fractional distillation.
A balanced equation has the same number of each type of atom on both sides.

sections.titre: Alkanes and alkenes: structure, formulae and tests
sections.contenu_markdown:
**Alkanes** are **saturated** hydrocarbons: all carbon-carbon bonds are single bonds. Their general formula is $\mathrm{C_nH_{2n+2}}$. **Alkenes** are **unsaturated** hydrocarbons: they contain at least one carbon-carbon **double bond**, $\mathrm{C{=}C}$. Their general formula is $\mathrm{C_nH_{2n}}$.

| Carbon atoms | Alkane | Alkene |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Methane, $\mathrm{CH_{4}}$ | none |
| 2 | Ethane, $\mathrm{C_{2}H_{6}}$ | Ethene, $\mathrm{CH_2{=}CH_2}$ |
| 3 | Propane, $\mathrm{C_{3}H_{8}}$ | Propene, $\mathrm{CH_3CH{=}CH_2}$ |
| 4 | Butane, $\mathrm{C_{4}H_{10}}$ | Butene, $\mathrm{C_{4}H_{8}}$ |

Alkane names end in **-ane** and alkene names end in **-ene**. Both families are insoluble in water and burn in oxygen. Methane is the main part of natural gas, and alkanes are separated from **crude oil** by fractional distillation.

**Alkenes are made by cracking.** Long alkane molecules from the heavier fractions are broken into shorter, more useful molecules, which include alkenes. Ethene can also be made by heating ethanol with concentrated sulphuric acid at about 170 $^\circ$C.

**Chemical test for unsaturation.** Shake the compound with **bromine water** (orange). An **alkene decolourises it**: orange to colourless. An alkane does not change it.

**Key difference in reactions.** An alkane is saturated, so it can only **substitute** one atom for another. An alkene is unsaturated, so it can add atoms across the double bond (**addition**), and many alkene molecules can join together (**polymerisation**).

variantes.quand_utiliser: When combustion or reaction with chlorine is asked
variantes.contenu_markdown:
**Combustion** in plenty of oxygen gives carbon dioxide and water: $\mathrm{CH_{4} + 2O_{2} \rightarrow CO_{2} + 2H_{2}O}$ In limited oxygen, poisonous carbon monoxide and soot form.

**Substitution.** An alkane reacts with chlorine in **ultraviolet light**. A hydrogen atom is replaced by a chlorine atom, and hydrogen chloride is the second product: $\mathrm{CH_{4} + Cl_{2} \xrightarrow{\text{UV light}} CH_{3}Cl + HCl}$ More hydrogen atoms can be replaced one by one: $\mathrm{CH_{3}Cl + Cl_{2} \xrightarrow{\text{UV light}} CH_{2}Cl_{2} + HCl}$ A substitution reaction always produces **two** products.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When an alkene reacts with hydrogen, bromine or steam
variantes.contenu_markdown:
In an **addition reaction** the double bond opens up and atoms add on. There is only one product.

**With hydrogen** (nickel catalyst, heated): $\mathrm{C_{2}H_{4} + H_{2} \xrightarrow{\text{Ni}} C_{2}H_{6}}$ This is used to make margarine from vegetable oils.

**With bromine:** $\mathrm{C_{2}H_{4} + Br_{2} \rightarrow C_{2}H_{4}Br_{2}}$ The orange bromine water turns colourless.

**With steam** (phosphoric acid catalyst, high temperature and pressure): $\mathrm{C_{2}H_{4} + H_{2}O \overset{\text{catalyst}}{\rightleftharpoons} C_{2}H_{5}OH}$ This is an industrial way of making ethanol.

**Combustion:** $\mathrm{C_{2}H_{4} + 3O_{2} \rightarrow 2CO_{2} + 2H_{2}O}$ Alkenes burn with a smokier flame than alkanes.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When plastics or cracking are asked
variantes.contenu_markdown:
**Addition polymerisation.** Many small unsaturated molecules (**monomers**) join to form one long chain (the **polymer**). The double bonds open and there is **no other product**.

$n\,\mathrm{CH_2{=}CH_2} \rightarrow \left(\mathrm{-CH_2-CH_2-}\right)_n$

Ethene gives poly(ethene), propene gives poly(propene), and chloroethene gives PVC. Poly(ethene) is used for bags and bottles, poly(propene) for ropes and buckets, and PVC for pipes. These plastics are **not biodegradable**, and burning them gives toxic gases.

**Cracking** breaks a long alkane into a shorter alkane and an alkene, using heat at about 500 $^\circ$C and a catalyst: $\mathrm{C_{10}H_{22} \rightarrow C_{8}H_{18} + C_{2}H_{4}}$ It gives more petrol and the alkenes needed for plastics.

sections.enonce_markdown: A hydrocarbon **H** contains 85.7% carbon and 14.3% hydrogen by mass, and its relative molecular mass is 42. ($A_r$: C = 12; H = 1.) (a) Calculate its empirical formula and molecular formula. (b) State whether H is an alkane or an alkene, and name it. (c) Describe what happens when H is shaken with bromine water, and write the equation.

etapes.action: Divide each percentage by the atomic mass.
etapes.justification: This gives the ratio of moles of atoms in 100 g.
Divide both numbers by the smaller one.
etapes.resultat_markdown: C : H $= 1 : 2$, so the empirical formula is $\mathrm{CH_{2}}$

etapes.justification: $\mathrm{C_3H_6}$ fits $\mathrm{C_nH_{2n}}$, the formula of an alkene, not $\mathrm{C_nH_{2n+2}}$.
An alkene adds bromine across its double bond.
etapes.resultat_markdown: Orange bromine water turns **colourless**. $\mathrm{C_{3}H_{6} + Br_{2} \rightarrow C_{3}H_{6}Br_{2}}$

sections.conclusion_markdown: H is **propene**, $\mathrm{C_{3}H_{6}}$; it decolourises bromine water by **addition**.

items.erreur_markdown: Alkenes are saturated because they have many hydrogen atoms.
items.pourquoi_faux: A saturated hydrocarbon has only single bonds. Alkenes have a carbon-carbon double bond and so hold fewer hydrogen atoms than the alkane with the same number of carbons.

items.erreur_markdown: Bromine water changes from colourless to orange when an alkene is added.
items.pourquoi_faux: The colour change is the other way round. The orange bromine adds across the double bond and is used up.
items.correction_markdown: Bromine water changes from **orange to colourless**.

items.erreur_markdown: Ethane reacts with chlorine by addition.
items.pourquoi_faux: Ethane is saturated, so it has no double bond to add across. It reacts by substitution in ultraviolet light, which forms hydrogen chloride as well.

items.erreur_markdown: The general formula of the alkenes is $\mathrm{C_nH_{2n+2}}$.
items.pourquoi_faux: $\mathrm{C_nH_{2n+2}}$ is the formula of the alkanes. An alkene has two fewer hydrogens.

items.erreur_markdown: Addition polymerisation makes the polymer and water.
items.pourquoi_faux: In addition polymerisation the monomers simply join up. Nothing is lost.
items.correction_markdown: There is only **one product**, the polymer.

items.enonce_markdown: (a) Write the molecular formula of the alkane with 6 carbon atoms and of the alkene with 5 carbon atoms. (b) Name $\mathrm{CH_{3}CH_{2}CH_{3}}$. (c) Which of the two types of hydrocarbon decolourises bromine water?
items.solution_markdown: (a) Alkane $\mathrm{C_nH_{2n+2}}$ with $n = 6$: $\mathrm{C_{6}H_{14}}$. Alkene $\mathrm{C_nH_{2n}}$ with $n = 5$: $\mathrm{C_{5}H_{10}}$. (b) **Propane**. (c) The **alkene** decolourises it, because it is unsaturated.

items.enonce_markdown: Poly(propene) is made by addition polymerisation of propene, $\mathrm{C_{3}H_{6}}$. ($A_r$: C = 12; H = 1.) (a) Write an equation for the polymerisation of propene using the symbol n. (b) A sample of the polymer has a relative molecular mass of 21 000. How many propene molecules joined to make one polymer molecule? (c) State two problems caused by discarded plastic bags.
items.solution_markdown: (a) $n\,\mathrm{CH_3CH{=}CH_2} \rightarrow \left(\mathrm{-CH_2-CH(CH_3)-}\right)_n$ (b) $M_r(\mathrm{C_3H_6}) = 36 + 6 = 42$, so $n = 21\,000 / 42 = $ **500** molecules. (c) They are **not biodegradable**, so they block drains and cause flooding and litter, and burning them gives **toxic gases**.

items.enonce_markdown: A gaseous alkene **X** has a relative molecular mass of 56. ($A_r$: C = 12; H = 1; O = 16; 1 mole of gas = 24 dm$^3$.) (a) Use the general formula to find the molecular formula of X. (b) Write equations for X with hydrogen (nickel catalyst) and with bromine. (c) A sample of 1.4 g of X is burnt completely in oxygen. Write the equation and calculate the volume of carbon dioxide and the mass of water formed.
items.solution_markdown: (a) $\mathrm{C_nH_{2n}}$ has $M_r = 12n + 2n = 14n = 56$, so $n = 4$ and X is $\mathrm{C_{4}H_{8}}$ (butene). (b) $\mathrm{C_{4}H_{8} + H_{2} \xrightarrow{\text{Ni}} C_{4}H_{10}}$ and $\mathrm{C_{4}H_{8} + Br_{2} \rightarrow C_{4}H_{8}Br_{2}}$ (c) $\mathrm{C_{4}H_{8} + 6O_{2} \rightarrow 4CO_{2} + 4H_{2}O}$ $n(\mathrm{X}) = 1.4 / 56 = 0.025$ mol. $n(\mathrm{CO_2}) = 4 \times 0.025 = 0.10$ mol, so $V = 0.10 \times 24 = $ **2.4 dm$^3$**. $n(\mathrm{H_2O}) = 0.10$ mol, so mass $= 0.10 \times 18 = $ **1.8 g**.

items_markdown: Alkanes: $\mathrm{C_nH_{2n+2}}$, saturated, single bonds only. Alkenes: $\mathrm{C_nH_{2n}}$, unsaturated, one $\mathrm{C{=}C}$ double bond.
Alkanes burn and undergo **substitution** (with chlorine in UV light), giving a halogenoalkane and HCl.
Alkenes undergo **addition** with hydrogen, bromine and steam; they decolourise bromine water (orange to colourless).
Many alkene molecules join by **addition polymerisation** to make plastics, with no by-product.
Cracking breaks long alkanes into shorter alkanes and alkenes; plastics are non-biodegradable.
